items.stem: When interpreting an image prompt, what should you consider first?
items.answer: The mood, possible stories and perspectives it suggests
items.markingKey: The mood, possible stories and perspectives it suggests. Interpretation drives creativity.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the perspective you choose matters.
items.answer: Perspective shapes what the reader knows and feels; an unusual viewpoint can transform a simple image.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Perspective shapes what the reader knows and feels; an unusual viewpoint can transform a simple image. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between its suggested meaning and the literal content of an image.
items.answer: The literal content is what is shown (a swing, fog); the suggested meaning is what it implies (absence, memory, loss).
items.markingKey: The literal content is what is shown (a swing, fog); the suggested meaning is what it implies (absence, memory, loss). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Look at this image: a moving van outside a block of flats at dawn; a child presses a hand against the van's window. Suggest three perspectives you could write from and the story each would tell.
items.answer: E.g. the child leaving (loss, hope); a friend watching from a balcony (abandonment); the van driver (an outsider noticing the moment). Credit three distinct perspectives with stories.
items.markingKey: E.g. the child leaving (loss, hope); a friend watching from a balcony (abandonment); the van driver (an outsider noticing the moment). Credit three distinct perspectives with stories.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a moving van parked outside a block of flats at dawn; a child presses a hand against the van's back window.]
Image 2: [A drawing: a staircase that spirals up into the clouds; at the bottom, a pair of school shoes has been left neatly side by side.]
Image 3: [A painting: a desert at night under a sky full of stars; a camel caravan's lanterns form a line of tiny lights.]

Choose ONE image. Plan a piece of creative writing: give a title, the form (story, diary, letter or speech), the opening hook, the turning point, the ending and the register you will use.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: diary entry or letter; narrator: a first-person child narrator; structure: the last morning – the journey – the first sight of somewhere new; techniques: present tense, lists of things left behind, a hopeful final line. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: diary entry or letter; narrator: a first-person child narrator; structure: the last morning – the journey – the first sight of somewhere new; techniques: present tense, lists of things left behind, a hopeful final line. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem: A student claims: "You must use every detail in the image." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Use the details that serve your idea; the image is a starting point, not a checklist.
items.markingKey: Use the details that serve your idea; the image is a starting point, not a checklist. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a crowded night market in Bangkok seen from above; one stall glows brighter than the rest, and a boy stands still in the moving crowd.]

Write a descriptive paragraph (about 150 words) that recreates this scene using at least three senses.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a busy, vibrant but slightly lonely mood; possible idea – a boy separated from his family, a stallholder's last night before the market closes, or a newcomer to the city; techniques such as sensory lists, contrast between motion and stillness, a shift in pace; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a busy, vibrant but slightly lonely mood; possible idea – a boy separated from his family, a stallholder's last night before the market closes, or a newcomer to the city; techniques such as sensory lists, contrast between motion and stillness, a shift in pace; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: "The best creative responses to images ignore the obvious interpretation." Discuss.
items.answer: Originality helps, but execution matters most; a familiar idea told with insight and control can outperform a strange but weak one.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: originality is rewarded; unexpected angles engage readers. Arguments against: an obvious idea, well executed, can be powerful; forced originality can feel artificial. Supported judgement: Originality helps, but execution matters most; a familiar idea told with insight and control can outperform a strange but weak one. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: snow falling on a market in Kraków; a stallholder pours hot chocolate for a girl who is counting coins.]
Image 2: [A painting: a desert at night under a sky full of stars; a camel caravan's lanterns form a line of tiny lights.]
Image 3: [A painting: a lighthouse on a black rock in a storm; its beam cuts across the waves towards a small boat.]

Choose ONE image. Explain what the image suggests about place, character and feeling, and outline one story it could start.
items.answer: Image 1: mood – cosy but poignant; ideas – a small kindness, a girl saving for a present, or a stallholder's memory of his own childhood | Image 2: mood – vast, peaceful and awe-inspiring; ideas – a journey to a new life, a young guide's first crossing, or an ancient story retold | Image 3: mood – dramatic and hopeful; ideas – a keeper guiding a boat home, a rescue told from the boat, or a lighthouse that is about to be switched off forever
items.markingKey: Indicative content (any image): Image 1: mood – cosy but poignant; ideas – a small kindness, a girl saving for a present, or a stallholder's memory of his own childhood | Image 2: mood – vast, peaceful and awe-inspiring; ideas – a journey to a new life, a young guide's first crossing, or an ancient story retold | Image 3: mood – dramatic and hopeful; ideas – a keeper guiding a boat home, a rescue told from the boat, or a lighthouse that is about to be switched off forever Marks: mood identified and justified from details (2); two plausible ideas (2); perspective explained (1).

items.stem:

Image 3: [A painting: a desert at night under a sky full of stars; a camel caravan's lanterns form a line of tiny lights.]

items.answer: circular structure
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of circular structure.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "A short story needs lots of plot events to be interesting." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Short stories work best focused on one key moment or change, developed in depth.
items.markingKey: Short stories work best focused on one key moment or change, developed in depth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a linear structure and a non-linear structure.
items.answer: A linear structure tells events in chronological order; a non-linear structure uses flashbacks, flash-forwards or fragmented order for effect.
items.markingKey: A linear structure tells events in chronological order; a non-linear structure uses flashbacks, flash-forwards or fragmented order for effect. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: two hands, one old and one young, holding the same chess piece above a board in a park in Moscow.]

Using this image as a stimulus, write about 300 words told by a third-person narrator.
items.answer: Indicative content: a final game between a grandfather and grandson, a rivalry between strangers, or passing on a skill; structure – the game begins – memories surface – the final move; techniques such as symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax; a tense but affectionate mood.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a final game between a grandfather and grandson, a rivalry between strangers, or passing on a skill; structure – the game begins – memories surface – the final move; techniques such as symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax; a tense but affectionate mood. items.stem: Write a short exchange of dialogue (four lines) that reveals tension between two siblings, correctly punctuated.
items.answer: Credit correct speech punctuation, new line for each speaker and subtext revealing tension.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Description is more important than dialogue in creative writing."
items.answer: Both are important; a balanced piece uses description for atmosphere and dialogue for character and conflict.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: description builds setting and mood; examiners reward vivid language. Arguments against: dialogue reveals character and creates pace; balance is key. Supported judgement: Both are important; a balanced piece uses description for atmosphere and dialogue for character and conflict.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "circular structure".
items.answer: A story that ends where it began, often with a changed meaning
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a story that ends where it began, often with a changed meaning. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a word limit affects structural choices.
items.answer: With limited words, writers must focus on one key moment and choose a structure (e.g. in medias res, circular) that maximises impact.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With limited words, writers must focus on one key moment and choose a structure (e.g. in medias res, circular) that maximises impact. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Explain how the ambiguous ending shapes this narrative, and how you could use a similar structural choice in your own writing.
items.answer: The ambiguous ending: we do not learn whether Thabo takes the reward; his gentle words suggest kindness comes first, leaving the reader to judge his motives.
items.markingKey: The ambiguous ending: we do not learn whether Thabo takes the reward; his gentle words suggest kindness comes first, leaving the reader to judge his motives. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "proofreading".
items.answer: Checking for errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: checking for errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a target and a strength.
items.answer: A strength is what the writing already does well (e.g. vivid sensory detail); a target is a specific improvement to make next time (e.g. vary sentence openings).
items.markingKey: A strength is what the writing already does well (e.g. vivid sensory detail); a target is a specific improvement to make next time (e.g. vary sentence openings). items.stem: A student claims: "Proofreading is not worth the time in an exam." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Even a few minutes of proofreading can correct errors that lower criterion D marks.
items.markingKey: Even a few minutes of proofreading can correct errors that lower criterion D marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following news report from a coastal newspaper in Kenya.

RECORD TURTLE HATCHING ON WATAMU BEACH
More than 1,200 green turtle hatchlings reached the sea from Watamu Beach on Saturday night, the highest number recorded in a single night since monitoring began in 1998.
Volunteers from Local Ocean Conservation guarded 14 nests for eight weeks.
"We were on our knees in the sand at 2 a.m., counting," said volunteer Amani Mwangi, 17. "Every single one made it past the crabs."
Experts warn that rising sand temperatures could reduce numbers in future years.

You have 10 minutes. Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) about "1,200 ... 14 nests for eight weeks", then say which criterion it most clearly meets.
items.answer: Precise figures: "1,200 ... 14 nests for eight weeks" – numbers make the report factual and credible.
items.markingKey: Precise figures: "1,200 ... 14 nests for eight weeks" – numbers make the report factual and credible. MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.markingKey: "It's been raining all day; Sam and I were stuck inside and we were bored." – it's; comma splices; "Sam and I"; "were".

items.stem: Under timed conditions (45 minutes), write a piece of 400–600 words inspired by an image of a hospital corridor at 3 a.m. Then write a short self-assessment against criteria B, C and D.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction story set on Mars.

The first child born on Mars turned twelve today. Her name is Hope, which everyone agrees was a bit much.
She has never felt rain. She has never seen a dog. When she watches old Earth films, she asks why people walk outside without helmets, as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world.
Tonight she stood at the dome window and pointed at a small blue dot. "Is that really where we're from?" she asked.
Nobody knew how to tell her that it was no longer safe to go back.

Annotate "it was no longer safe to go back" with two techniques and their effects, then rate your annotation against criterion A (0-8) with a reason.
items.answer: Foreshadowing / revelation: "it was no longer safe to go back" – the final line reveals a disaster on Earth, turning curiosity into tragedy.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Soweto, South Africa, in 1976.

The new rule came on a Monday: half our subjects would now be taught in Afrikaans. Mathematics. Geography. A language most of our teachers barely spoke.
Thabo tore the notice from the classroom door. "They want to teach us in the language of the people who made the pass laws," he said.
I said nothing. I was fourteen and I wanted to pass my exams.
By June I was marching beside him, holding a cardboard sign: WE ARE NOT AFRAID. My hands were shaking so much the letters blurred.

Explain how the time jump from Monday to June shapes this narrative, and how you could use a similar structural choice in your own writing.
items.answer: The time jump from Monday to June: compressing months into a paragraph break shows how quickly the narrator's perspective changes.
items.markingKey: The time jump from Monday to June: compressing months into a paragraph break shows how quickly the narrator's perspective changes. Write a narrative or descriptive piece (400-600 words) inspired by ONE image. Your piece should show a clear perspective and a deliberate structure.

items.markingKey: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; a first-person narrator; structure: the missed bus – opening the bag – an unexpected consequence; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: an elderly woman and a teenage girl sit on a train platform in Mumbai, sharing earphones; the departures board shows "DELAYED".]
Image 2: [A photograph: an empty playground swing still moving in thick fog; a single red glove lies on the wet tarmac.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a single lit window in a tall dark tower block at midnight; a silhouette is holding a sign against the glass that says "HELLO?".]

Choose ONE image and use it as the starting point for a piece of imaginative writing (400-600 words). Give your piece a title.
items.answer: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a grandmother and granddaughter on their last journey together, a delayed train that changes a decision, or music that bridges generations; a first-person teenage narrator; structure: waiting and irritation – shared song and memory – departure; techniques such as dialogue to reveal character, a symbol (the shared earphones), a flashback. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image.

Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "subtext (in an image)".
items.answer: What an image suggests beyond what it literally shows
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: what an image suggests beyond what it literally shows. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What is a circular structure?
options: A story that ends where it began
items.answer: A story that ends where it began
items.markingKey: B. Returning to the opening shows change.

items.stem: Explain why practising timed writing improves exam performance.
items.answer: It builds speed, helps students judge how long planning, writing and checking take, and reduces anxiety.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It builds speed, helps students judge how long planning, writing and checking take, and reduces anxiety. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why it is useful to brainstorm several story ideas from one image.
items.answer: The first idea is often the most obvious; generating several lets the writer choose the most original and developed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The first idea is often the most obvious; generating several lets the writer choose the most original and developed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a flashback can be effective in a short story.
items.answer: It reveals important background or motivation at a key moment, adding depth without a long chronological build-up.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It reveals important background or motivation at a key moment, adding depth without a long chronological build-up. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A vague target such as "write better" helps improvement." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Effective targets are specific and linked to criteria (e.g. "use at least three different sentence structures for effect").
items.markingKey: Effective targets are specific and linked to criteria (e.g. "use at least three different sentence structures for effect"). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A painting: a desert at night under a sky full of stars; a camel caravan's lanterns form a line of tiny lights.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a girl in a football kit stands alone in a stadium tunnel, looking towards the bright pitch.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a schoolbag left on a bench at a bus stop in heavy rain; the bus's red tail-lights disappear around the corner.]

Choose ONE image. Explain what the image suggests about place, character and feeling, and outline one story it could start.
items.answer: Image 1: mood – vast, peaceful and awe-inspiring; ideas – a journey to a new life, a young guide's first crossing, or an ancient story retold | Image 2: mood – nervous and expectant; ideas – a first match after an injury, a trial for a national team, or proving a doubter wrong | Image 3: mood – frustrated and lonely; ideas – a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion
items.markingKey: Indicative content (any image): Image 1: mood – vast, peaceful and awe-inspiring; ideas – a journey to a new life, a young guide's first crossing, or an ancient story retold | Image 2: mood – nervous and expectant; ideas – a first match after an injury, a trial for a national team, or proving a doubter wrong | Image 3: mood – frustrated and lonely; ideas – a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion Marks: mood identified and justified from details (2); two plausible ideas (2); perspective explained (1).

items.stem: "A short story needs lots of plot events to be interesting." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Short stories work best focused on one key moment or change, developed in depth.
items.markingKey: Short stories work best focused on one key moment or change, developed in depth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a Gothic short story told by a teenage narrator.

My brother says I imagine things. He's probably right. I imagined the scratching behind the wallpaper. I imagined that the mirror in the hall shows the room as it was a hundred years ago – the gas lamps, the dark curtains, the woman in grey.
Last night I imagined she turned round.
This morning there were wet footprints on the stairs. Small ones. Bare.
My brother says I must have walked in my sleep. I didn't tell him that my feet were dry.

Annotate "Small ones. Bare." with two techniques and their effects, then rate your annotation against criterion A (0-8) with a reason.
items.answer: Short fragments: "Small ones. Bare." – the fragments slow the reader and force attention onto each disturbing detail.
items.markingKey: Short fragments: "Small ones. Bare." – the fragments slow the reader and force attention onto each disturbing detail. MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: the hands of a street musician in Buenos Aires playing an old accordion; coins and a handwritten sign that says "For Mamá" lie in the case.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a single lit window in a tall dark tower block at midnight; a silhouette is holding a sign against the glass that says "HELLO?".]
Image 3: [A photograph: a moving van parked outside a block of flats at dawn; a child presses a hand against the van's back window.]

Choose ONE image and plan a creative piece of 400-600 words. State your form and audience, your narrator, a three-part structure and two language techniques you will use, with a reason for each.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person passer-by narrator; structure: ordinary rush hour – the music stops someone – a small act of kindness; techniques: sound imagery, a shift in perspective, understatement. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person passer-by narrator; structure: ordinary rush hour – the music stops someone – a small act of kindness; techniques: sound imagery, a shift in perspective, understatement. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a single lit window in a tall dark tower block at midnight; a silhouette is holding a sign against the glass that says "HELLO?".]

Using this image as a stimulus, write about 300 words told by a first-person neighbour narrator.
items.answer: Indicative content: a call for help, a game between neighbours, or loneliness in a big city; structure – noticing the sign – replying – meeting the person; techniques such as suspense, an epistolary element (signs as messages), a gentle twist; a mysterious and lonely mood.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a call for help, a game between neighbours, or loneliness in a big city; structure – noticing the sign – replying – meeting the person; techniques such as suspense, an epistolary element (signs as messages), a gentle twist; a mysterious and lonely mood. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: Plan how you would divide 60 minutes for a creative writing task of 400–600 words.
items.answer: E.g. 5–8 minutes interpreting the prompt and planning; 40–45 minutes writing; 5–10 minutes proofreading and editing.
items.markingKey: E.g. 5–8 minutes interpreting the prompt and planning; 40–45 minutes writing; 5–10 minutes proofreading and editing.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The best creative responses to images ignore the obvious interpretation."
items.answer: Originality helps, but execution matters most; a familiar idea told with insight and control can outperform a strange but weak one.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: originality is rewarded; unexpected angles engage readers. Arguments against: an obvious idea, well executed, can be powerful; forced originality can feel artificial. Supported judgement: Originality helps, but execution matters most; a familiar idea told with insight and control can outperform a strange but weak one.

items.stem: Write a narrative of 400–600 words inspired by an image of a robot vacuum cleaner stuck against a door in a dark flat. Use a deliberate structure and at least one passage of dialogue.
items.answer: Indicative content: an imaginative interpretation; consistent perspective; deliberate structure (e.g. circular, in medias res); purposeful dialogue; vivid description; accurate punctuation of speech. Criteria B, C, D.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: an imaginative interpretation; consistent perspective; deliberate structure (e.g. circular, in medias res); purposeful dialogue; vivid description; accurate punctuation of speech. Criteria B, C, D.

items.stem:
Read the following sequence of three haiku, "Monsoon Morning".

First fat drops of rain –
the dusty street holds its breath,
then the whole sky falls.

Children in puddles
splash the grey world into gold –
school bags overhead.

Evening. Frogs begin
their loud green orchestra; the
drains sing all night long.

Write a sequence of three haiku about a season or type of weather in your own country, moving from morning to night.
items.answer: Indicative content: three haiku in 5-7-5 form (allow minor variation); each captures one precise image; a sense of time passing; at least one figurative device.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: three haiku in 5-7-5 form (allow minor variation); each captures one precise image; a sense of time passing; at least one figurative device. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).
